title: Wallabies gear up for mouthwatering South Africa clash: ‘A massive, massive Test’ | Jack Snape - The Guardian
content: With Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the wing and a bench packed with forwards, coach Les Kiss is hoping he has a formula to topple the Springboks The weight of the occasion is almost enough to tip the great red continent into the Indian Ocean. Sunday night’s clash between the Wallabies and South Africa in Perth marks a year from the start of the home World Cup, which will kick off with the Wallabies playing at the same venue. The date with the mighty Springboks is also the first match under Wallabies coach Les Kiss against one of the traditional rugby powers. It’s also the country that happened to give the Australian his first opportunity coaching in union more than two decades ago. The former North Sydney Bears winger has not shied away from big decisions in his selection, only adding intrigue to already hefty anticipation. “This is a big, big Test team, [and] everyone knows they go three, four deep in every position,” Kiss said, continuing a buildup more befitting a weighbridge. “We expect nothing but a massive, massive Test match against them.” Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, who has worn the heavy expectations of the Australian rugby community for two years, has finally been shifted to wing. Kiss said he made the move partly to defuse the bombardment expected by a side that alternates blows high and low. “[Suaalii’s] aerial battle is going to be big,” Kiss said. “He’s probably one of the best in the business.” The coach further explained that Len Ikitau’s ability to play No 12 and 13 – where the centre will start on Sunday – as well as Hunter Paisami’s own versatility and strong form, also facilitated the move. The change could a signal of a change in tack, however, with the World Cup just 12 months away. Suaalii’s modest impact at outside centre has had many in Australia rugby believing one of the Wallabies’ aces has not yet found the perfect hand, and calling for a redraw. Suaalii said recently that he was keeping an “open mindset” to his position, and Kiss said the player was “nothing but positive” this week when told of the move. The coach still expects the former NRL star – who is just 23 but has already made 24 Wallabies appearances – to return to centre at some point in the match when reserve winger Harry Potter is called on, and was adamant he remains an option in midfield. “I didn’t even have to explain some of the rationale around it or the reasons why we went that way, but he was up for it, no doubt,” Kiss said. “When I spoke to him originally, [he said he will] put the jersey on, play anywhere – and I know they all say that – but to tell you the truth, I’m really happy with him at 13, I am.” Suaalii’s first start at wing is Kiss’s most notable selection, alongside his decision to pack the bench with forwards. They number six, one more than the traditional 5-3 split, and are designed to counter the Springboks’ finishing group which includes the front row which started the last two Tests against the All Blacks. “You look at what they’re finishing with and you can see the idea that Rassie [Erasmus, South Africa’s coach] has come in with. But we’ve got a pretty good bench too.” The latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewed The Springboks look different from the team that finished off New Zealand in Baltimore two weeks ago. That 43-28 win secured the series 3-1. Flanker Pieter-Steph du Toit and centre Damian de Allende have been allowed to fly home. Erasmus has made 13 changes from the starting side he selected in Baltimore, and backrower Siya Kolisi, centre Jesse Kriel and prop Thomas du Toit have been left out of the 23. Only lock Eben Etzebeth and winger Ethan Hooker retain their places in the XV. Rather than expose weakness, however, the unorthodox selection showcases the depth of the world champions. Starting props Zachary Porthen, 22, and Jan-Hendrik Wessels, 25, were good enough to be named on the bench for the first Test against the All Blacks, won by New Zealand 33-16, but did not play again in the series. Two-time World Cup winner Handrè Pollard has been recalled at flyhalf, having also missed the past three Tests, and inside centre André “the giant” Esterhuizen – who doubles as a flanker – will captain the Springboks for the first time. Erasmus said in the lead-up he will use Sunday’s clash to test the depth of his squad. “We rolled the dice a little bit against the All Blacks by [selecting] consistently the same team,” he said. “We obviously were getting some momentum as [the series went] on longer, but if we keep on doing that, how would we know when we get to the Nations Championship at the end of the year, or at the World Cup next year, what can the next guy do?” Kiss described Erasmus, with whom he worked in Ireland, as a “deep thinker” and a “good mate”, as well as someone who will “have a few things up his sleeve, that’s for sure”. But so too might the Australian, whose first experience of elite rugby union was with the Springboks as defence coach when Erasmus, now 53, was still playing. “I learned rugby through the eyes of Springboks,” Kiss said. “That’s just the plain truth of it all. I loved the Wallabies, I saw the way we play, the skilful nature of our game, the way that we would use the ball on the back of [John] Eales and co taking that forward pack forward. “So I knew the game, I understood the tenets of the game and how it worked, but when you’re on the ground and you learn the game through the eyes of the Springboks, it was a powerful way to learn first up. I often say it was a gift, to learn rugby through their eyes.”

title: Kasia v. Demi: Worlds Provided Another Chapter in One of Cycling’s Great Rivalries - Outside Magazine
content: The battle between Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma at the 2026 UCI World Championship had shades of women’s cycling history all over it. For the past five seasons, women’s cycling has been marked by their showdowns. While others have entered the fray, in the key moments it seems to always come back to them. In Montreal, that was once again on display. Riders attacked, breakaways went, but in the end it had to be them—Demi and Kasia—till the end. On the line, Vollering took the win, as she seems to do more often than not, but Niewiadoma rode a patient, calculated race. That showed in a sprint that was neck and neck until Vollering pulled away in the final 30 meters. It was a postcard example of what happens when two top competitors keep finding themselves in scenarios where they must beat one other. “In the end, your greatest competitors are also like your greatest motivation,” Vollering said after the race. “I know Kasia will be chasing me, so for the next time I always need to train harder. In the end, we keep pushing each other to another level. “That’s what you need in sports. I think what we show today is incredible and the level we show is amazing.” On the surface, it is easy to look at the Vollering versus Niewadoma and see the imbalance that exists on the results sheet. By the numbers, Vollering wins much more. Yet, great rivalries don’t need to be a fifty-fifty split. If the riders are different enough, imbalance can be part of the push and pull of the narrative. It can also push the riders to try and approach the racing from a creative perspective. For Vollering and Niewadoma, there are enough chapters in the rivalry where that inspiration can be found in many different places. Niewadoma even used her 2023 UCI Gravel Worlds Championships win over Vollering as a reference point to how she could beat her in Montreal. “I was reminding myself in the last four or five weeks when preparing for today that I have beaten Demi and I won a world championship jersey,” Niewadoma said after the race. ”So why not do it again? “I feel like it’s something that gives me the belief, because sometimes when you’re on such a high level, it’s less about physical abilities, and more about mental abilities. Like, how much you believe in yourself, how much you’re willing to feel that confidence that drives you further. “We’re all very strong and it’s all that mental game that you have playing in your mind in the last kilometers.” That really is the juice that drives great rivalries. It is not tit-for-tat equality. It is about the legacy of years of battles and the familiar beats of action that both the fans and competitors know very well. Add in a dynamic where one rider has a clear advantage in one aspect of racing, and the result can be thrilling: an underdog story between the best riders in the world. Between Vollering and Niewadoma, Vollering’s sprint is one of those key imbalances. For Niewadoma to win, she would have to be perfect. In the end, she nearly was. A flying Elisa Longo Borghini made for an unpredictable finish. The Italian helped Niewadoma pull Vollering back after she attacked and then kept the pressure on the leading duo as she chased them in the final throws of the race. That set up the right finishing scenario for Niewadoma to try and sit on Vollering’s wheel and kick around her on the final rise to the finish. After the climb, it was all about that mental battle that defines the rivalry for Niewadoma. More than that, it was a chance for the Polish rider to try and regain that confidence that came from her dominant win on Mount Ventoux in the Tour de France Femmes. “On the second-to-last stage [of the Tour de France Femmes] when I lost the yellow jersey, that’s where I cracked slightly mentally,” Niewadoma said. “Once you’re on the wave of feeling good and getting what you want, your confidence is very high. “But the confidence doesn’t last. It is such a fleeting thing. You constantly have to work for it. So today was a new opportunity for the result.” For an instant in the sprint, it looked as if Niewadoma was about to take that opportunity and swing the momentum of the rivalry back in her favor. She kicked well and was pushing Vollering. Yet, Vollering fought back, and cramps in the last 50 meters decided the race in the Dutch woman’s favor. Vollering finally had the rainbow jersey that had eluded her, coming good on her status as pre-race favorite. Yet, even with another result added to Vollering’s growing resume, the battle cemented once again how powerful the rivalry is. “I think this is one of the most beautiful races we have ever shown,” Vollering said of where this race stood in the history of their battles. “I couldn’t switch off at any moment. I needed to stay super focused every single second to make sure nothing crazy would happen. “I felt that today was an incredible race and one of the prettiest races we have shown.”

title: Trump flyover and Secret Service checks greet fans at marquee Texas v Tennessee clash - The Guardian
content: Air Force One flies low over Neyland before kickoff Schools coordinate with Secret Service over headsets Encouraging fans to get inside Neyland Stadium earlier than usual with Donald Trump coming to Tennessee’s college football game against Texas sure worked Saturday. Security checks on the stadium’s perimeter went relatively smoothly with Tennessee officials opening the stadium 30 minutes earlier than normal. Fans got half-price off concessions as a reward for showing up early, and Tennessee faithful had the stands half full 90 minutes before kickoff and nearly packed an hour before. Those in their seats were treated to a low-altitude flyover by Air Force One as the US president came into town with the Volunteers and Longhorns warming up on the field below. Trump landed at 11.28am ET ahead of the noon kickoff, according to reporters traveling with the president. Trump’s motorcade arrived at Neyland Stadium just as the national anthem was being sung at 11.59am. Trump pumped his first a couple times when shown in his seat on the videoboards with Tennessee’s US senators on either side. One of them, Marsha Blackburn, is running for governor of Tennessee. The president’s motorcade left at 2.07pm with the game in the second half. Colin Simmons tied the program record with five sacks as top-ranked Texas went on to hold off No 14 Tennessee 20-17. The president’s visit did not appear to affect communications between coaches and players on the field thanks to some coordination before Saturday’s game. Longhorns coach Steve Sarkisian said earlier this week that teams had to be ready to lose all communication on their headsets between coaches on the field and the players “anytime [Trump] enters the stadium, leaves the stadium or changes locations within the stadium.” This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. ABC/ESPN reported Saturday that both schools worked with the Secret Service on audio channels in hopes of keeping communications clear, noting an official timeout for a serious disruption could be an option. The Southeastern Conference matchup between the Longhorns and Volunteers in Knoxville already was one of the biggest games in the country this weekend. Trump came to watch Texas quarterback Arch Manning play for the first time in the stadium where his uncle Peyton became famous. Trump has attended more college football games than any recent sitting president, and he arrived in Knoxville in the midst of a midterm election season and a heated debate over the role of money in college sports that Congress is trying to resolve. He has attended national championship games and regular season contests in the SEC and Army v Navy. He also attended Game 3 of the NBA finals between the New York Knicks and San Antonio Spurs in June, went to the 2025 Daytona 500 car race, and presented the World Cup trophy to Spain at the final in July. And last year, he was the first president to attend a Super Bowl. He left the Super Bowl after half-time. Headset communications emerged as the latest subplot surrounding this presidential visit. Coaches communicate with each other on their headsets throughout the game and also call in plays to the quarterback. Disruptions to those communications, from a deafening crowd, technical glitch or presidential security measure, can present problems for coaches and teams. Coaches involved in last season’s College Football Playoff championship between Miami and Indiana in New Orleans cited that game as an example of how Trump’s movements affected them. Trump left in the fourth quarter of a tense Indiana 27-21 victory. Sarkisian said Miami coach Mario Cristobal told him Trump’s leaving at that point disrupted communications on the Hurricanes’ final possession, which ended with a game-clinching interception. Indiana coach Curt Cignetti disputed Sarkisian’s version of events around the final drive. But Cignetti noted communications briefly cut off in a key moment of the fourth quarter as Indiana was trying to protect their lead. In his weekly radio show on Thursday, Cignetti recalled that when Trump left the game “around the seven-minute mark ... there were two or three plays we couldn’t hear at all.” That included a misdirection touchdown run by Miami’s Malachi Toney. “Communication device came back right after the [Toney’s] touchdown,” Cignetti said. “And we had no problem the rest of the game.” According to the media pool report of Trump’s movements at the game, the president left the stadium with “with just under 8 minutes left in the 4th quarter”. The White House on Friday insisted Trump’s departure caused no problems for the teams. “No, President Trump’s departure from the CFP championship in January did not cause headset or comms issues for the teams,” the White House posted on X. It’s unclear if Trump’s presence at other games like the Super Bowl have created issues. An NFL spokesman declined comment Friday when asked if league officials work with the Secret Service when a president attends a game like the Super Bowl to minimize any impact on team communications. University of Tennessee officials sent a midweek advisory encouraging fans to arrive “significantly earlier” than for a typical game. Neyland Stadium has an official capacity of 101,915 with this game the 30th consecutive sellout. Fans were warned of the Secret Service conducting enhanced screening at the stadium gates and to “expect increased wait times as kickoff approaches”.

title: Ireland v Israel: Day of infamy exposes serious lack of leadership in FAI - The Irish Times
content: Not even the most pessimistic forecasts of the reality of playing Israel could have foreseen a day as abject and rancorous as this. It began at 9.56am, when the FAI press officer sent a WhatsApp message to an Irish journalist to say Ireland’s press conference, due to start in 19 minutes, would be postponed by around two hours until after their 11am training session. Uefa’s match delegate learned about the delay at the same time as the media. At 10.40am, the Israel FA press officer told us that the Irish training session would be delayed, as he had been told that the Irish team had not yet left the team hotel. The Irish players would not leave their hotel for another four-plus hours. They were holed up together in a fraught meeting, arguing about whether they should play Israel. The players met on Friday in Pristina to come to a collective stance as to what to do around the match. An eleventh-hour boycott was not on the agenda – instead they planned to air their views and come to a unified position around the prematch protocol such as handshakes. They planned to draft and publish a statement after the meeting, in advance of the Saturday morning press conference. The meeting was tense and acrimonious, running so long that the FAI delayed the departure of their charter flight to Hungary. Saturday dawned and still the players’ statement had not been published. It needed unanimous sign-off, and unanimity did not exist. Gavin Bazunu declined to approve the statement when asked by the FAI to do so on Friday night, telling them he would talk to them on Saturday morning. Bazunu awoke on Saturday and sought a meeting with Hallgrímsson, and told him he did not want to be involved in the Israel game. Bazunu said he did not want to withdraw from the squad and would make himself available against Austria next Thursday, but his conscience would not allow him to face Israel. Bazunu’s decision led some players to consider whether to withdraw with him. The total number of players who considered withdrawing is not yet known, with conflicting numbers emerging across the day. At 12pm, with the Irish squad still in their hotel, the Irish media abandoned the stadium to pitch up outside the team hotel. A few Israeli journalists came in tow. TV cameras and microphone stands were assembled outside the hotel door, while the team bus stood outside, empty aside from its local driver, who looked bored and perplexed. At one point an FAI security guard came out to the bus driver, told him something, and returned to the hotel. When we asked him whether the team would be going to training, he theatrically shrugged his shoulders to tell us he didn’t know. Armed police outside the hotel erected a cordon in front of the assembled press, while FAI security smiled half in apology as they escorted hotel guests inside. A couple of local fans sat outside with sour faces, flicking listlessly through the Irish player photographs they had brought along in the hope they would get autographed. We looked at a glossy photo of Caoimhín Kelleher holding the Premier League trophy in a Liverpool shirt and told her that she had picked a bad day to go autograph hunting. An Irish fan hung in the background to the whole scene, wearing a white Irish jersey and a black-and-red cap bearing the logo of the Kosovan Liberation Army. Journalists sweated beneath the fierce sun and sighed the strange sigh of weary disbelief that is the mark of people who watch the FAI for a living. We wondered whether the FAI would become the first sporting organisation in history to boycott something accidentally; not so much taking a stand as a stumble. Our phones rang with requests from international media outlets, asking what was happening and whether the game would go ahead. Having met with chief executive David Courell and then among themselves, the players sat in meetings with Hallgrímsson and staff. At 1pm, the players emerged from their conclave, barely visible to us through the narrow gaps between partitions in the window. The players spoke with their families, friends and agents seeking their counsel as to what to do. Some asked how withdrawing from the game might affect their careers at club level. One source close to an Irish player said that the situation had become so difficult that the Irish Government should step in and make the decision for the players. Some turned on Bazunu, one of whom is understood to have abused him directly to his face. Finally, at 2.20pm, an Israeli journalist yelled to us that the Israel FA had been told the Irish team would be training at the stadium at 3.45pm. After hours of ignored calls and messages, the FAI communications department confirmed this when we asked them, adding that the press conference would be held 15 minutes prior. They did not confirm whether the game would go ahead. The media scrambled into Ubers back to the stadium where at 3.30pm, Heimir Hallgrímsson finally appeared. He was accompanied not by a player but by CEO David Courell and director of football John Martin. President Paul Cooke, the head of the delegation and the elected representative of the FAI’s General Assembly, was nowhere to be seen, consistent with his message to the Irish press back on Wednesday that it would be “unlikely” that he would do media this week. That no member from the FAI board on whom this decision rests appeared before the media is breathtaking. Courell read from a prepared statement, apologising for the delay to the press conference. He explained that one player had said that morning that they did not want to be involved in the Israel match – he did not name Bazunu – and that this led to another round of talks among players as to what they should do. Courell described Bazunu’s decision as “a new variable that required time and deliberation among the squad.” Courell said that at around 90 minutes earlier, the players balloted on whether to proceed with the game. He said there was a “a significant majority” in favour of playing the game, and so the game would go ahead. He persistently refused to divulge the precise result of the vote. When one journalist said he understood that the vote was 14 in favour and eight against and asked if that was true, Courell replied, “a significant majority can be open to interpretation.” Courell also said the players would not be speaking to the media at all for the rest of the international window; would make a charitable donation that will be supplemented by the FAI; that the players would wear black armbands during the game in recognition “for all lives lost in the conflict”; and that they would refuse to shake hands with the Israeli players and coaching staff. John Martin sat hunched and silent to Courell’s left, while Hallgrímsson sat to his right, looking wan and almost dissociated. The manager spoke in a low, abashed tone, and when harangued with questions by Israeli media, he was left alone to answer questions about Hamas and his decision to work in Qatar, and later about Ireland’s 1936 match against Nazi Germany. None of Courell, Martin, nor the press officer stepped in. Hallgrímsson resiled from his use of the word genocide last week, saying he was echoing a slogan used by one of the boycott advocacy groups, “don’t play ball with that word.” His comments, he said, were intended to convey that playing against Israel did not endorse their politics. It was an excruciating scene, with Hallgrímsson at one point talking his way into an endorsement of some social reforms led by the late Emir of Qatar. We asked Courell how the FAI had allowed it all to come to this, and whether he believes his position as CEO was still tenable. He launched into an epic filibuster – at one point explaining the concept of the FAI’s general assembly for the benefit of the Israelis present – before he eventually revealed the FAI had spoken to around 30 players in advance of the camp to gauge their feelings on playing Israel. They based this list on players’ recent record of caps, and Bazunu was not among the people to whom the FAI spoke. Hallgrímsson then revealed that he had not spoken to Bazunu in advance of the camp after he was named in the squad. Hallgrímsson said last week that he had spoken to every player he called up and asked for their feelings on playing Israel, but now he said he had only spoken to the outfield players. So, extraordinarily, neither the head coach nor an executive at the FAI had a conversation with Bazunu in advance of this week to ask him about how he felt about playing Israel. Shortly after the press conference ended, the Irish players appeared on to the pitch for training, five hours and 15 minutes later than billed. The Uefa match delegate asked the stadium staff to put the standard 15-minute countdown on the stadium screens to indicate the portion of the session to be open to the media, and then punched the air in relief. Israel turned up exactly on time for their press conference at 6pm, with their head of communications reading his own pre-prepared statement. He said the FAI and the Irish players had belatedly come to the right decision, as “the separation of football and politics must be maintained,” adding that Uefa, the Israel FA, and the FAI had “stood together” to avoid the politicisation of football. He said the Israelis would be offering their hands to the Irish players on Sunday night, and added an addendum that Israel has asked Uefa to reverse the sending off against Austria of their player Saied Abu Farchi, who got a second yellow card for grabbing the corner flag and making a gesture that some interpreted as mimicking a rifle. The Israel FA said he was actually pretending to make a snooker cueing action, “like the legendary Ken Doherty.” The chief result of all of this is that Ireland will play Israel on Sunday night, but the ramifications of this abject day will be long-lasting, and the toxicity of the fallout may come to rival Saipan. Bazunu has been left brutally isolated, any semblance of squad unity has been utterly sundered, the head coach looks bewildered, matchgoing fans are already voicing their disgust, and the FAI has been humiliated before the watching world. There is genuine anger towards Bazunu by some members of the Irish squad and staff for his decision, as if his withdrawal was responsible for this chaos; that without his decision they would have arrived at a satisfactory compromise to continue the FAI policy of merely trying to get through this mess without too many mishaps. [ ‘It would be wrong to participate’: Gavin Bazunu on decision to withdraw from squad for Israel matchOpens in new window ] But Bazunu is not responsible for any of this, because everything that happened across this day of infamy is a direct consequence of a serious lack of leadership from the Government, Uefa, and ultimately the FAI. All of these bodies allowed the most bitterly contentious news story of modern times to cascade down upon a group of players, forcing them to wrestle with their conscience and careers beneath a torrent of extreme public criticism and pressure, and all before the eyes of the world. The FAI hoped to wing their way through this fortnight but today collided with its brutal reality. The fallout is only beginning. Irish football has once again shown the world the importance of leadership by its unforgivable absence. title: Nations League: Who made an uncharacteristic error? England player ratings v Spain - BBC
content: England were beaten 3-2 in an entertaining game by world champions Spain in the Nations League - the Three Lions' first match since this summer's World Cup. Lamine Yamal gave Spain the lead before goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put England ahead. Kane then missed a penalty before Alex Baena curled in to level the score, with Mikel Oyarzabal scoring the winner. Here's how we rated England's players - and you can have your say in the comments at the bottom. James Trafford: Showed early on his ability to play with the ball at his feet but conceded after just two minutes when Guehi gifted the ball to Lamine Yamal. An important save stopped Torres making it 2-0 in the first half. 6 Jarell Quansah: Continued at right-back after showing what he could do in the position at the World Cup. A physically dominant performance and had a chance to score but headed over. 6 Ezri Konsa: Some shaky moments for Konsa and England's back four but the centre-back regrouped and got better as the game went on. 6 Marc Guehi: An uncharacteristic error gifted the ball - and the opening goal - to Lamine Yamal. 5 Nico O'Reilly: Put in the cross for Kane's goal as England took the lead in the first half. Did a good job of trying to deal with Lamine Yamal. However he gave the ball away for Spain's second goal. 6 Elliot Anderson: Nearly punished for giving the ball away in a dangerous position in the first half but Ferran Torres rolled his shot wide. Anderson and midfield partner Lewis-Skelly took some time to settle in what was a tough night in the middle of the pitch against a Spain side who moved the ball so well. 6 Myles Lewis-Skelly: A first England start in centre midfield for Lewis-Skelly after shining for Arsenal. Given the tough task of trying to shut off the supply to Spain's conductor, Rodri. A solid performance. Replaced after 70 minutes. 6 Jude Bellingham: The Real Madrid midfielder produced another dominant display and was unlucky to be on the losing side. He provided an assist for England's equaliser and won a penalty which Kane hit against the bar after slipping. Stung Simon's palms with a drive in stoppage time. 8 Bukayo Saka: Won a couple of free-kicks around the box and shot over from the edge of the area in the first half. Curled just wide with the score level but a quiet night for the winger. 6 Anthony Gordon: The Barcelona winger scored an excellent goal on the counter-attack. He kept calm when played through on goal by Bellingham when his pace put him clear. A dangerous cross in the first half after England went behind and a threat in behind all night. 8 Harry Kane: Started dropping deep in the first half in search of the ball after England went behind. Scored the second with a deflected header to put England in the lead but missed a penalty when they had the chance to add a third in the second half. 7 James Garner (on 70, Lewis-Skelly): Took on Lewis-Skelly's role of trying to keep Rodri quiet. 6 Morgan Rogers (on 70, Gordon): Did not get much of the ball in his 20 minutes on the pitch. 6 Morgan Gibbs-White (on 83, Saka): Came on and played on the left wing. 6 Calvert-Lewin (on 83, Kane): Not much time to impact the play. 6 Jarrad Branthwaite, (on 89, Guehi): A late change for Guehi in the England backline. No time to make an impression. 6 Subs not used: Pickford, Steele, Alexander-Arnold, Scott, Chalobah, Hall, Eze. title: Spain extend unbeaten run after thriller with two comebacks v 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 - Yahoo Sports
content: England really did try in front of their home crowd at Wembley. But the current Euro and World Cup champions EXTENDED their unbeaten run. Spain, the record-holder, are now 39 matches unbeaten — 30 wins and nine draws. They have not been beaten since March 2024, when they lost to Colombia. There were TWO comebacks in the thriller that opened Group A3 in League A of the Uefa Nations League. The 3-2 had plenty of key moments, a blunder, decisive VAR intervention, and a missed penalty. Guéhi failed to notice Yamal, made a terrible mistake, and watched the No. 19 strike ruthlessly after 1 minute and 47 seconds. The only thing they did not count on was Ferran Torres' poor finishing. He had two BIG chances to extend the lead after being picked out by Yamal and then Rodri. But he failed to deliver. Thomas Tuchel's England managed to "grow into the game" as the minutes passed. Then came the counterattack that started after Nico Williams slipped. The comeback came shortly after, when Kane got on the end of O'Reilly's cross and benefited from a deflection off Cucurella (40'). The "Barça x Real" clash between Rodri and Bellingham ended with VAR awarding a penalty. Kane stepped up, but slipped and smashed it against the bar — and the No. 9 also made two touches. Luis de La Fuente brought on Álex Baena and Oyarzabal — and they would make the difference. The Atleti midfielder had already set up Yamal nicely before making it 2-2 in the 60th minute. Spain's greater ability to control the ball and find spaces brought another positive consequence. Laporte found Baena, who set up Oyarzabal. And the Sociedad striker beat Trafford with real class (74'). England kept pushing in the final minutes. But Spain held firm. title: Munster v Glasgow: Five takeaways as 'Scottish bench makes crucial difference' with 'fierce rivalry reignited' - Planet Rugby
content: George Horne was a match-winning influence for Glasgow and, inset, Munster coach Clayton McMillan After a 26-20 victory for Glasgow over Munster in their United Rugby Championship (URC) clash at Thomond Park on Saturday, Planet Rugby selects five takeaways from the opening-round action in Limerick. This was a lively contest where the outcome left the visiting Glasgow jubilant. It was only 12 minutes from time when the winners finally hit the front, and their joy was unconfined after they went on to clinch a four-try bonus point just before the finish. The Scottish bench made the crucial difference, its impact eclipsing Munster’s 10-point interval advantage, and by the time the final whistle sounded, the hosts couldn’t really complain as they had run out of gas and the level of infringement spun out to a damaging level. It was Munster who had got the scoreboard moving with JJ Hanrahan’s early penalty kick punishing an offside, and they went on to ‘win’ the Ollie Smith deliberate knock-on sin-bin 7-0 with a neatly executed 14th minute try. Hanrahan’s 50:22 kick presented a lineout opportunity, and the resulting strike play featuring Ben O’Donovan on the wraparound ended with Ben O’Connor easily making it to the line. Glasgow’s attack was essentially non-existent, and they were relying on a couple of turnover penalties to keep their defence intact, with Munster’s confidence growing in their snappier brand of play. The Warriors eventually woke up, and a 31st-minute converted maul try, finished off by Jamie Dobie’s snipe, cut the gap to three points. However, the visitors then fell foul of referee Morne Ferreira, and the consequence was a 36th-minute converted try from Michael Milne for a 17-7 interval advantage. This was reduced to three again when sub Nathan McBeth finished off a 51st-minute attack founded by fellow replacement Seb Stephen’s dance through the cover. The margin was pushed out to six through Hanrahan’s 58th minute penalty kick, but Glasgow then took complete control after a scrum penalty came their way four minutes later. Dobie’s break fractured the Munster defence on 68 minutes to invite George Horne to dive over and the winger was scoring himself eight minutes later to settle the result and reward the pressure instigated by Brian Gleeson’s ruck penalty concession. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Following last season’s discontent on and off the pitch, Clayton McMillan’s second season in charge was viewed as a fresh start for Munster. There will be grievances over how they faded in the closing 20 minutes; losing at home is never an easy thing to swallow, but there were green shoots in the opening hour that will give optimism. Of particular interest was their decision to have two new assistant coaches, Jared Payne and Mossy Lawler, in charge of the attack. While Munster appeared to run out of ideas with their bench failing to add second-half energy and impetus, their first-half approach was refreshing. They were up to mischief right from the off, swiftly attacking from a scrum on halfway to reach the opposition 22, and the advance tempted Glasgow offside at the cost of three points. Plenty more examples materialised to highlight how their approach to using the ball has been finessed, and their handling skills also looked sharper. For instance, there was a smart O’Connor offload on hitting the ground to the supporting Hanrahan after the winger had gobbled up a Kyle Rowe kick and countered. Time will be needed to make even more of an improvement, but this first glimpse was decent. It had them in a winning position before they visibly tired and the penalty count against them became a wounding, unmanageable 15-8. Lions v Leinster: Five takeaways as ‘Gunne shots fired’ in Johannesburg but ‘mischief-making’ wingers have decisive say Coming off the back of a season where their double trophy dream was firebombed by home losses to the Bulls (21-20 in URC) and to Toulon (22-19 in Europe), getting over the off-season hump can’t have been comfortable for ambitious Glasgow. An incredible amount of hard work getting themselves into great seedings for the play-offs had gone up in smoke and for a long time in Limerick, it seemed as if there was a hangover lingering into this new campaign. Their respected attack play came across as clunky and ineffective, but the upside to Glasgow’s useful habit of winning way more games than they lose under Franco Smith is they have an ability to keep calm in the knowledge that they can often turn backs-to-the-wall situations around. That was certainly the case here. Munster had bounced into the interval, buoyed not only by their lead but also by how they had stopped a Glasgow maul producing a score in the final play. That fizz should have kept them bubbling when the match resumed, but instead it was Glasgow who knew what they were about and understood how to manipulate the situation they were in. There were momentum-shifting scrum penalty wins, and they also had a clutch of players who carried harder than what Munster could offer. It said a lot about the energy-sapping contest they created that five home players had to make 20 or more tackles, whereas the busiest visiting tackler was credited with 16. Add in the potency of Horne and Dobie when it came to exploiting even the tiniest of gaps and the mix became too much for McMillan’s side to cope with. Warriors’ ambition was such that instead of going for the posts for a certain three points to extend their lead to four, they had the swagger to kick to the corner and turn the ensuing pressure into a try on the other side of the pitch. Well played. Sharks v Ospreys: Five takeaways as ‘real deal with real wheels’ shines along with ‘last-minute Purchase’ It was January 2016, eight months after they had clashed in the 2015 league final in Belfast, when a fierce rivalry between Munster and Glasgow really ignited. The Irish accused the Scots of skullduggery, repeatedly targeting the standing leg of Conor Murray, and the niggle carried over into an October follow-up in Europe where Munster’s Keith Earls was red-carded. Munster’s recent decline had diluted the needle, but Saturday’s collision fired things up again. The South African ref had already issued a warning to both teams over their use of foul language, and a spiky row then followed before the interval. With Munster debutant Kieran Brookes awarded a scrum penalty after a Glasgow put-in, scrum-half O’Donovan went to wrestle the ball from Horne to try and tap and go. This face-off resulted in Matt Fagerson shoving O’Donovan over from behind, an intervention that sparked the schemozzle that ended with Glasgow penalised another 10 metres on top of the scrum penalty award, and a warning was also aired that the incident was “not true to the values of this game”. It was costly for the visitors, as Munster were soon burrowing over for their second try after the play restarted, but the dust-up was a reminder that these two clubs do not like each other. Bulls player ratings: ‘Terrific’ playmakers take control while star midfielder ‘breaks down’ defence in Italy It’s only one round of matches, but the sight of all four Irish provinces getting defeated this weekend suggests this URC campaign is going to be incredibly hard-fought. Munster versus Glasgow in Limerick, Ulster versus Edinburgh in Belfast and Connacht versus Stormers in Galway all resulted in away victories, and hat-trick title-chasing Leinster also took a blow to the nose as they lost out by a point to the Lions on the road in South Africa. It is a rare sight to see all four Irish occupying places on the table outside the league’s top eight. While of course it is very early days in an 18-match regulation URC season, next weekend’s response will be intriguing. Connacht are away to Benetton on Friday night, with Leinster at the Sharks, Ulster at Glasgow and Munster hosting the Bulls on Saturday looking for results that will leave round one of the 2026/27 edition written off as a rare blip rather than an indication of a collective downturn. title: Hyundai Ioniq V Drives Over 400 Miles on a Single Charge, It Would Be the Cheapest EV in America - autoevolution
content:
The UFO lookalike Hyundai Ioniq V will be available in three distinct configurations, with the base starting at 119,900 yuan, which translates to $17,600, while the range-topping variant is a $139,900-yuan deal ($20,840). These prices would position it not only as the cheapest EV in America, but also the cheapest car in the U.S. right now. The most affordable zero-tailpipe-emission vehicle here is the Chevrolet Bolt, starting at $28,995, followed by the Kia EV3 with a starting price of $29,890, and the Nissan Leaf, which kicks off at $29,990. In the meantime, the Hyundai Venue stands as the cheapest car in the U.S., at $20,550, which is still more expensive than the base Ioniq V. Eight exterior colors are available, with the Cyber Gold, Dimension Purple, and Gamma Green being the most daring. Sitting on Hyundai's E-GMP architecture, the Ioniq V measures 192.9 inches (4,900 millimeters) in length, 74.4 inches in width, and 57.9 inches (1,470 millimeters) in height, sitting on a wheelbase of 114.2 inches (2,900 millimeters). These figures make it similar in size to the Hyundai Ioniq 6, which is also marketed in the United States. In the meantime, the 66.8-kWh battery pack can make the Ioniq V drive as far as 404 miles (650 kilometers) in ideal conditions before it needs to be plugged in again. However, those numbers are achieved in the very generous Chinese testing cycle (CLTC). The very strict EPA would slash roughly 25% to 30% off that range if the model had made it to America. Designed at the Hyundai China Design Center and built at the Beijing Plant 3 in China by Beijing Hyundai, the Ioniq V will be a global model, which is likely to make it to select European markets as well as the Middle East, but Hyundai has yet to determine the export strategy for the model. The Hyundai Ioniq V is the automaker's first step in Hyundai’s China strategy. Hyundai is planning to launch no fewer than 20 battery electric and extended-range electric models over the next five years, targeting yearly sales of up to 600,000 units by 2030. title: Storylines | Royals v. Courage: A Clash Between Two of the League’s Top Scoring Sides - Real Salt Lake
content: Utah Royals FC host North Carolina Courage FC at America First Field in its second of two home matches. The Royals will look to maintain its position at the top of the table and complete the sweep over the Courage. This edition of Storylines will look at how the Royals’ have been able to keep opponents off balance defensively, and what to expect against the league’s best goal scoring team. Last time against North Carolina, the Royals broke the NWSL record for most set piece goals scored in a single game with four. The orchestrator behind two of those set piece goals was Spanish defender, Nuria Rábano, who recorded her first multi-assist game as a Royal. Since arriving from VfL Wolfsburg in the beginning of the 2025 season, Rábano has become an instrumental part of the Royals incredible turnaround. The Spanish defender is becoming a focal point this season as more teams plan to contain the offensive firepower provided from Cloé Lacasse and Mina Tanaka. Head Coach Jimmy Coanraets spoke highly of Rábano’s offensive capability with a wicked left-foot able to send in a dangerous cross from any position on the field. He also talked about how her initial delivery off set pieces and corner kicks has contributed to the Royals scoring the joint third most set piece in the league with eight. In the match against the Courage, Rábano’s first assist came directly off a deeply swung corner kick toward the back post, where captain Kate Del Fava applied the finishing touch to give the Royals a 1-0 lead in the 6th minute. Her second assist of the match came off a reworked corner where she lofted a threatening ball from outside the penalty area into the six yard box that was finished off by the outside boot of Tatumn Milazzo. Rábano’s last assist was on September 12th against Houston Dash, when she crossed a low driven ball into the penalty area where Tanaka scored a tap-in at the far post for the game winning goal. Rábano has recorded a career high four assists this season while generating 36 scoring chances and the second most chances off of set pieces with 12. The Courage looked to generate strong momentum after scoring in the 55th minute, however a stunning header by Tanaka ended North Carolina’s hope of securing a win. The fourth set piece goal came after Lacasse won and converted a penalty kick in second half stoppage time to seal all three points for the road team. The Royals are looking to complete its third sweep of the season, the other two sweeps are Houston Dash and Orlando Pride. Since returning to the NWSL in 2024, the Royals are 2-2-1 (W-L-T) against the Courage with neither side having completed a sweep against each other. Earlier this week, Coanraets talked about shutting down North Carolina’s top goal scorer and the NWSL Golden Boot leader, Ashley Sanchez. Since facing off against the Royals on July 25th, Sanchez has scored ten goals in ten games and has contributed toward seven goals in her last four away games (5 goals, 2 assists), with at least one goal involvement in each of those matches. title: USMNT v Peru: How to watch, TV channels & live stream Saturday 26 September - The Guardian
content: How will the USA and Peru fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options The 2026 World Cup and the abrupt exit to Belgium in the last 16 is behind the US men’s national team, with Mauricio Pochettino naming several uncapped youngsters on his roster as a new cycle begins. Christian Pulisic, Weston McKennie, Folarin Balogun and a few other established figures have been left off the roster. The USMNT will use matches against Peru, Chile, Mexico and Canada to set a new direction for the future. Peru are entering a rebuilding phase after failing to qualify for this year’s World Cup and are similarly aiming to use this friendly in Orlando to set the tone for a successful next cycle. Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s international friendly, including kick-off times, broadcast networks and online streaming options. The lack of experience in Pochettino’s squad is particularly stark in the attacking ranks, where Damion Downs is the only forward with a cap to his name. Cole Campbell, Justin Ellis, Julian Hall and Cavan Sullivan are all uncapped. Other youngsters such as Mathis Albert, Zavier Gozo, Neil Pierre, Brooklyn Raines and Frankie Westfield could be in line for debuts. title: Uefa Nations League today: How to watch England v Spain, TV channels & live stream Saturday 26 September - The Guardian
content: How will England and Spain fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options Thomas Tuchel still hasn’t been forgiven by a large swath of the England support who remember how the German’s game management contributed to the Three Lions’ collapse against Argentina in the World Cup semi-final this summer. The England manager has a point to prove, making Saturday’s Nations League opener something of a referendum on his continued employment. A defeat and a poor performance would add to the noise around Tuchel. Spain have no such problems. Indeed, Luis de la Fuente and his players are still basking in the glow of World Cup glory and have another opportunity to demonstrate why they’re the team to beat in international soccer. Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s Uefa Nations League fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks and online streaming options. Tuchel must show he can evolve England’s playing style. At the World Cup, his team played a generally conservative game that cost them in the semi-finals, when Argentina fought back to get the better of their historic rivals. Tuchel bore the brunt of the criticism for his tactical choices. The selection of Trent Alexander-Arnold and Morgan Gibbs-White suggests Tuchel is willing to release the handbrake, although the withdrawals of Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento due to injury limited his options. Spain’s squad is stacked with talent in all areas with Pedro Porro the only member of the team that started the World Cup final unavailable for the trip to Wembley. The world champions will control the majority of the match, limiting England to quick transition moments. Player to watch: Ferran Torres, Spain – The forward who scored the winning goal in the World Cup final has started the season in exceptional form. Torres has found the net seven times in six games for Paris Saint-Germain and could carry that form into Saturday’s international outing.

title: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game - BBC
content: FAI chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the Republic of Ireland squad in protest Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture. Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the squad before the match. But he added that a vote among the squad produced a "significant majority" in favour of playing. As well as the intention to wear black armbands for Sunday's 'away' game against Israel in Debrecen, Courell said the players will make further gestures for the initial game and the return 'home' fixture against Israel next Sunday in Serbia. The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3. Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace. "One of their requests is to remove their media obligations for the remainder of this window," Courell said at Saturday's delayed news conference. "They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict. "There will be elements of the pre-match ceremony not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland and it is also the intention of the players to make a significant contribution to charitable donation by virtue of both [Israel] match fees and also the fixture against Austria at the Aviva [Stadium in Dublin on Thursday]." FAI CEO David Courell delivers a statement before Israel game There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place. A pre-match news conference with manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player, scheduled for 09:15 BST, was postponed just 15 minutes before it was scheduled to start, with reporters informed it would instead take place after the team's training session which was also delayed. The players were locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged a player, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding. About 13:00, players began to filter out of the meeting room, with it then confirmed the news conference would indeed go ahead, back at Nagyerdei Stadion at 14:30, with training to follow. More than five hours after the initial news conference was scheduled to begin, Courell - flanked by Hallgrimsson and FAI director of football John Martin - confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game. "This morning, a player expressed their discomfort at the fixture and indicated their intent to withdraw," Courell said. "This new variable required time for the rest of the squad to consider and what proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly among the players, but also at times with coaching staff and the [FAI] executive. "There were a lot of positions presented and the association is fully respectful of everyone's right to their respective opinion." Later on Saturday, Bazunu posted on social media explaining his decision, one that he said he had "not taken lightly". "I am a man of strong faith and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel," he said. "My decision is based purely upon my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. "It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israel people or the Jewish community but against the atrocities in the region. "There are few times when you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger and I strongly believe that this is one of them." Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious Republic of Ireland squad will meet to discuss Israel games 'It's a situation you can't win' - Heimir Hallgrimsson Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott of the fixtures. The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. Hallgrimsson relayed that nobody "can understand the pressure that has been going on these players" and said the lengthy meeting on Saturday stemmed from "a change of mind for one of the players to play the game". "All of the rest of the players are training today," he confirmed. "The balance [to play] changed with this [withdrawal] and obviously it was an ongoing discussion but we came to a conclusion and the game is going ahead. "We will train and there will probably be more discussions tonight and probably tomorrow. It's a unique situation and we are just trying to limit the damage." The Republic of Ireland lost their opening Nations League fixture in Kosovo on Thursday, a match overshadowed in the build-up by the Israel games. Asked whether the far from ideal preparation for Sunday's game would affect the players, the Irish boss said "we will see". "Nobody is comfortable but it's about limiting the damage, both personally and for Irish football, that we need to find some solution on it," Hallgrimsson added. "There is no action we do that everyone will agree to, so we need to find a solution to limit the damage for us as a group, for Ireland as a nation and the association for football in Ireland. "We don't know the consequences if we don't play the game but a lot of players share a common feeling, so there are two choices and both are tough. It's a situation you can't win." A spokesperson for the Irish governement insists any decision regarding the fixtures lie firmly at the door of the FAI and Uefa. "The FAI had decided to play the fixtures against Israel in accordance with their obligations as members of Uefa. Following engagement with players today decision stands," they said. "The FAI has strongly represented the views of its membership that Israel should be excluded from international football competitions, including bringing a motion to Uefa to this effect last year. The reality is that this motion was not passed by Uefa and that the FAI was obliged to fulfil the fixture." Israel FA's director of communications Shlomi Barzel confirmed they will appeal Sayed Abu Farhi's red card in the 3-1 defeat by Austria Israel Football Association [IFA] head of communications Shlomi Barzel commended the Republic of Ireland team for confirming they will play, saying "football has won". Barzel began Israel's news conference with a statement before requesting  questions regarding the game-only were directed towards captain Dor Peretz and head coach Ran Ben-Shimon who remained on script. "The separation between football and politics must be maintained, any other approach spell chaos," he said, confirming Israel players intend to shake hands before the game. "The Irish football association [FAI] and the national team players did he right thing by recognising this, even if it took a bit longer than it should. Yet, it is better to be late than never. "The one who certainly lost today are those who want to intimidate to separate and turn the football pitch into a political arena. Uefa, the IFA [Israel Football and the FAI stood strong together to prevent it." Barzel also confirmed the IFA intend to appeal both yellow cards shown to Sayed Abu Farhi in Thursday's 3-1 defeat by Austria. Abu Farhi was shown a second yellow for his goal celebration which Barzel insists was not mimicking the firing of a gun, but an "imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty." title: Hilton overwhelms Irondequoit as Lipani ties Section V coaching record - 13wham.com
content: Hilton's Jha’Zae Dessources (3) celebrates during the Cadets’ victory over Irondequoit on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Joel Balthaser/Pickin' Splinters) What was the final score of Hilton vs. Irondequoit? How many coaching wins did Lipani achieve to tie the record? Why did Lipani downplay his record-tying achievement? Hilton, N.Y. — Homecoming at Hilton High School, Cadets coach Rich Lipani told his team, is very much a Friday Night Lights affair at LeBeau Field. “He said in this community, homecoming is the football game,” senior running back and defensive back Tyler Reger said. Which means for the players wearing the Hilton uniform, you’re expected to put on a show, to uphold the tradition of hard-nosed, never-quit football that Lipani brought to Hilton his first year as head coach in 1989. It was mission accomplished for the Cadets (4-0) on Friday night. They scored touchdowns on their first six possessions, led 44-0 at halftime and cruised to a 58-7 victory over Irondequoit (2-2). In doing so, the players gave Lipani his 229th coaching victory, which ties the Section V record held by Dave Whitcomb. Predictably, Lipani downplayed the accomplishment. “It means I’ve been doing this a long time and if I didn’t have a lot of wins, I’d be doing a crappy job,” Lipani said. READ MORE.

title: Alice V. Cheney Siefert Obituary - Star-Gazette
content: It is with heavy hearts that we announce the peaceful passing of Alice Virginia Cheney Siefert, MSN-RN of Horseheads, NY formerly of Ft. Wayne, IN on September 18, 2026, after an acute illness. Alice, lovingly known as "Aunt Ai' or Nana, was born on July 24, 1939 in Corning, NY. She was the daughter of the late Guy William Cheney and Catherine Gelinas Cheney. In addition to her parents, Alice was pre- deceased by her loving husband, Dr H. Jack Siefert, her brother Guy William Cheney II, nephews Guy William Cheney III, Daniel Cheney, and her great niece Madison Naquin. She spent her early adulthood doing what she loved the most, becoming an RN and receiving her Master's in Corning, NY until she took a position in California as the head of nursing. This is where she met the love of her life - Jack. Alice was a firecracker and a straight shooter, two things he loved most about her. Eventually, Alice relocated to Fort Wayne, IN after she accepted a position as Vice President of Patient Care at Parkview Hospital. After she retired, they began travelling the world together for the next 37 years, visiting family, spending time in Montana, and experiencing countless other countries together. No matter where the adventure took them they would always find their way home to Fort Wayne at their house by the lake. Alice is known around her beloved neighborhood as the "dog lady,"  always having the best treats in her pocket on one of her morning or evening walks around the block. Alice loved to paint, bird watch, garden, ski, and host parties or holidays with the people that she cherished. So many of her beautiful pieces of artwork are found throughout friends and families houses. Her gardens consisted of variations of flowers with rocks scattered throughout from all of her travels with Jack. Thanksgiving at Aunt Ai's house was a family favorite, cooking together, making her sugar cookies, and surrounding the table to hear stories of their travels. Countless cherished memories were made at Aunt Ai and Jack's house. Alice is survived by her Nieces and Nephew, Christina Volpi, Katherine Mann (Ted), Ed Cheney (Michaelle), and Melissa Cheney, Extended family, Cheryl Siefert, Karen Siefert, Paul Siefert (Bonnie), and many grandchildren, great nieces and nephews. Services will be held at  St. Peter & Paul’s Cemetery in Elmira, NY on Saturday October 10, 2026 at 11 AM.  Rev. John De Socio will officate. Arrangements are entrusted to the LYNCH FUNERAL HOME 318 WEST BROAD STREET HORSEHEADS, NY. Words of Condolence and Memories may be shared at www.lynchsfuneralhome.com  . content: Scotland kick off a new era under Sebastien Pocognoli as the Tartan Army face Slovenia in the Nations League. The 39-year-old former Belgium international Pocognoli was a left-field replacement for Steve Clarke, who resigned following Scotland's group-stage exit form the World Cup. LIVE! He has promised a more energetic, front-foot style of play as Scotland look to the future and build up to Euro 2028, when they will be co-hosts. title: Republic of Ireland confirm rescheduled news conference before controversial Israel game - BBC
content: The Republic of Ireland will now hold their delayed news conference at 14:30 BST before they face Israel in tomorrow's Nations League fixture in Hungary - a fixture campaigners have called on them to boycott. Heimir Hallgrimsson's team are scheduled to meet Israel in Debrecen at 19:45 BST, with the return fixture in Backa Topola, Serbia on 4 October. They have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace. Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott. However, there are also Irish supporters, perhaps less vocal, who have always believed that the match should be played with supporters in attendance. Following Thursday's 1-0 defeat by Kosovo, midfielder Jason Knight opined he didn't think "the game should be going ahead", while winger Chiedozie Ogbene urged the public to not "put the pressure on us" regarding their approach to the scheduled game. Hallgrimsson and a player were scheduled to meet the media at 09:15 BST (10.15 local time), before training, but the conference was delayed shortly beforehand. A Uefa official entered the room to inform waiting media teams that the press conference was postponed until after training, which would have been about 11:30 BST (12.30 local time). But shortly afterwards, the Uefa official returned to the media room to announce that the Republic of Ireland's training session had also been postponed. Players were locked in a meeting at the team hotel with unconfirmed reports goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu had withdrawn from the fixture with several others considering their positions. However, just around 13:00 BST, the players began to emerge from their meeting room with it soon confirmed they would travel back to the stadium for the planned news conference with training scheduled for 14:45 BST. Reporters have now gathered out side the Republic of Ireland team hotel The fixture has been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3. A team meeting took place on Friday for players to air their views on Sunday's game and the return fixture in Serbia. The players were expected to release a statement at Saturday's news conference, but the delay has added further uncertainty, with some reports of at least one player wishing to withdraw from the squad. It has since emerged the news conference, scheduled to take place at the stadium, is now set to be staged at the team hotel, with Uefa unable to provide information regarding the delay. The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. title: Frank Warren believes Fury v Joshua fight will go ahead after threat of collapse - The Guardian
content: Tyson Fury says Anthony Joshua is ‘trying to pull out’ Frank Warren believes the proposed fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will still take place in Cardiff in December despite widespread concern on Saturday that the bout could be on the brink of collapse yet again. Warren, who has promoted Fury for years, told the Guardian: “It will still happen because the Saudis will sue the arses off them if it doesn’t. The Saudis are putting up the money. They’re the paymasters and so I think it will happen.” On Saturday morning, Fury had suggested that the fight was in serious jeopardy: “Breaking news. Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn are trying to pull out of this fight. They’re saying they’re not gonna fight now. It’s mainly to do with Eddie Hearn’s ego. He’s making up a million different things and threatening ‘we’re not gonna fight, we’re not gonna fight, we’re not gonna fight’. He’s cost us the biggest fight in boxing history. Clown.” Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. Hearn, who promotes Joshua, disputes the legitimacy of Dana White’s involvement in the much-hyped showdown between the two British former world heavyweight champions. White, the American combat sports promoter who made his name as the head of the UFC, the mixed martial arts business which he still runs, recently moved into boxing. White and his new company Zuffa Boxing have been named as co-promoters of the Fury-Joshua fight alongside The Ring, which is owned by Saudi Arabia and Turki al-Sheikh, the powerbroker who controls elite boxing. It had seemed likely for months that the fight, which is being funded by Netflix, would be staged at Madison Square Garden in New York in November. But Hearn and Joshua resisted those plans because of a clause in the original contract which had stipulated that the bout would be held in the UK. They were also concerned about the tax implications if Joshua fought in America and a protracted standoff eventually resulted in the switch to the Principality Stadium in Cardiff. In an interview with iFL TV, Hearn stressed that White’s involvement “ain’t happening” despite the American being described as a co-promoter in the Netflix press release on Thursday. Hearn added that “Dana White cannot be involved with this fight promotion. Netflix clearly didn’t get the memo. No one talks to each other. “Netflix say the fight is in conjunction with Dana White. Now we have to go through that process and deal with it. It’s a little bit annoying but, as I’ve shown through the UK battle that we won, we stand by our contracts.” The Cardiff location was confirmed on Thursday with an agreement from the city council in the Welsh capital that the fight will begin around 2am on the morning of Saturday 12 December. That time suits Netflix and their dominant home market in the US. “It will be a late start but that’s no different to fights we had for Joe Calzaghe and Ricky Hatton in the past,” Warren told the Guardian. “At least it’s in the UK. Let’s get on with it. Who cares about all this other rubbish? I don’t care if Dana White is sitting there. Who gives a monkeys?” Warren is frustrated by Hearn’s latest reaction, which he believes is driven by ego, and he stressed that, like many boxing fans, he is tired of the constant doubts and delays. He has worked with the event organisers Sela in securing the venue, and dealing with local authorities in Cardiff, but Warren has kept his distance from the tortuous negotiations between Hearn, al-Sheikh and White. A proposed contest between Fury and Joshua has been discussed for more than 10 years and subject to multiple postponements and cancellations. The two heavyweights are both long past their fighting prime but this week was meant to have confirmed their agreement to finally meet in the ring. Now I’m coming home. The Gypsy King is coming back to the United Kingdom to thrash you in front of all my fans in Wales, you absolute little nugget, bodybuilding sausage.” The two fighters are meant to face each other at the first official press conference in London this coming Wednesday evening and Warren believes Fury and Joshua will be there. A spokesperson for Hearn’s Matchroom Sport responded with a wry, and a little weary, “no comment” when contacted by the Guardian.

Inadequate preflight planning, poor preflight inspection, and an attempt to take off above a Cessna Citation V’s mtow with snow-contaminated wings led to a runway overrun on Dec. 27, 2024 at Stevens Field Airport (KPSO) in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, according to a newly released NTSB final report. The overweight, contaminated wings likely kept the airplane from rotating at the pilot's calculated speed, and by the time she rejected the takeoff, the airplane was already above decision speed. The planned Part 91 flight was bound for Tulsa Riverside Airport (KRVS) in Oklahoma, but ended when the airplane ran off the end of Runway 1 at KPSO. The light jet ran into the grass, damaging both wings; the two pilots and eight passengers were not injured. According to the NTSB, the pilot's type rating required a qualified second-in-command (SIC), but the copilot held no such rating and, by his own account, did not meet the requirements to act as SIC. The pilot told investigators that she was aware the copilot had no flight experience in type but assumed he was properly trained based on his job at a flight simulator training provider. The airplane’s lease agreement required the lessee, a passenger aboard the flight, to hire “professionally trained and qualified” pilots. But according to the lessee, the management company that operated the airplane, Metroplex Flight Services, arranged the pilots itself and asked only for a passenger count, never for passenger or baggage weights. Passengers told NTSB investigators that the flight crew filled every exterior luggage compartment, loaded a stroller into the lavatory and a child’s car seat into an empty passenger seat, and let each passenger keep a personal bag at their seat. The pilot calculated weight using ForeFlight’s standard average passenger weights—205, 184, and 87 pounds respectively for men, women, and children—for the five men, four women, and one child aboard, plus an estimated 130 pounds of baggage in the rear compartment and 110 pounds in the nose, arriving at a calculated payload of 1,285 pounds. Weights for each bag were determined by “heaviness,” not scales, the NTSB said. The pilot told investigators the airplane’s takeoff weight was about 15,700 pounds, equal to mtow. After the accident, a passenger gave investigators additional figures, including about 100 pounds of luggage inside the cabin and roughly 240 pounds for three dogs aboard, bringing the total reported weight of people, animals, and baggage to 2,154 pounds. Using that information, investigators calculated the airplane’s actual takeoff weight at about 16,502 pounds, some 600 pounds over the 15,900-pound mtow, with the center of gravity near its forward limit and likely outside the operating envelope. The pilot said she performed a standard preflight inspection and noticed only liquid water on the wings, with no icing or other contamination. Airport surveillance video, however, showed snow already accumulating on the wings as the pilot and copilot walked out to the airplane, and continuing to fall as passengers boarded. One passenger said FBO personnel, working with a handheld brush because the airport had no deicing capability, cleared the wings three separate times over about 11 minutes. According to the copilot, the pilot performed a tactile check of the wings after all passengers were loaded, but video showed no such check on the airplane’s right wing—the only wing visible on camera—after the final snow removal. Contamination remained visible on the wings as the airplane began taxiing, the ramp pavement was wet, and the snowfall rate appeared to increase once the airplane left the ramp. About 20 minutes passed between the last time snow was brushed from the wings and the start of the takeoff roll. The report cited FAA Advisory Circular 135-17, which states that snow or frost can reduce wing lift by as much as 30% and increase drag by 40%. The pilot gave conflicting accounts of what followed. She initially said the airplane accelerated normally through the 96-knot decision speed and 103-knot rotation speed, but did not rotate despite full aft deflection of the control yoke. Later, she told investigators that the airplane did not seem to accelerate at the expected rate. Data downloaded by the NTSB from the airplane’s Garmin GTN 750 avionics units showed it reached 120 knots indicated airspeed and 138 knots ground speed before the pilot rejected the takeoff with maximum braking and full reverse thrust. That is above the speed that FAA guidance describes as “the maximum speed by which a rejected takeoff must be initiated to assure that a safe stop can be completed within the remaining runway.” The airplane ran off the end of the runway, continued into the grass, and pivoted left before stopping. Passengers and crew exited and were met by airport emergency personnel. A post-accident examination found no evidence of pre-accident flight-control or engine anomalies that would have precluded normal operation.

title: Brown Named Semifinalist for William V. Campbell Trophy - georgiastatesports.com
content: ATLANTA — Georgia State senior quarterback Cameran Brown has been named one of 206 semifinalists for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy®, the National Football Foundation (NFF) & College Hall of Fame announced Wednesday. Celebrating its 37th year, the Campbell Trophy recognizes the nation's premier football scholar-athlete for combined academic success, football performance and exemplary leadership. Brown was selected as Georgia State's sole nominee for the award and joins a record-setting group of 206 semifinalists from across all NCAA divisions and the NAIA. The group includes 95 student-athletes from the Football Bowl Subdivision. The senior quarterback has continued to lead the Panthers both on and off the field in 2026. Through three games, Brown has completed 61-of-90 passes for 725 yards and four touchdowns while completing 67.8 percent of his attempts and posting a 143.4 efficiency rating. Brown has accounted for 819 yards of total offense through the first three games of the season, representing 53.5 percent of Georgia State's 1,531 total yards. Most recently, Brown turned in his best passing performance of the season at UCF, setting season highs with 30 completions, 47 attempts, 282 passing yards and two touchdown passes. Brown opened the season by completing 15-of-20 passes for 190 yards and two touchdowns in Georgia State's win over North Carolina A&T on Sept. 4. He connected with DJ Murray for a 30-yard touchdown for the Panthers' first score of the season. The William V. Campbell Trophy semifinalists are nominated by their respective institutions, with each school limited to one nominee. Candidates must be a senior in their final year of eligibility or a graduate student or graduate transfer who has already earned a degree, maintain a cumulative undergraduate GPA of at least 3.2, be a significant contributor on the football field and demonstrate strong leadership and citizenship. This year's 206 semifinalists boast an average GPA of 3.64, with 98 having already earned their bachelor's degrees. The group also features 130 team captains, 24 All-Americans and 114 all-conference selections. The Campbell Trophy is part of the NFF National Scholar-Athlete Awards Presented by Fidelity Investments, now in its 68th year. The program has recognized 954 individuals and will surpass $13.5 million in postgraduate scholarships with this year's awards. The NFF will announce 12 to 16 finalists on Oct. 21. Each finalist will receive an $18,000 postgraduate scholarship and become a member of the 2026 NFF National Scholar-Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments. The finalists will be honored at the 68th NFF Annual Awards Dinner on Dec. 8 at the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas. One finalist will be selected as the recipient of the 37th William V. Campbell Trophy and will have his postgraduate scholarship increased to $25,000. The Campbell Trophy was first awarded in 1990 and has become one of college football's most prestigious honors for achievement on the field, in the classroom and in the community. title: Texas v. Kennedy Abandons Federal Commitment to Community Integration - Autistic Self Advocacy Network
content: September 24, 2026 — Yesterday, the federal judge in the case of Texas v. Kennedy entered an order throwing out the community integration provisions of the Section 504 rule issued in 2024 by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The order applies across the country. The Defend Community Integration Coalition (DCIC) condemns the federal government’s action resulting in this order, and urges renewed advocacy to protect our right to community integration. The agreement approved by the judge was proposed jointly by the Department of Justice (DOJ) on behalf of HHS and the states of Texas, Florida, Alaska, Louisiana, and Montana. It affects only certain parts of the 2024 rule. The case is now closed. Learn more about Texas v. Kennedy at this link. While the DOJ/HHS and states’ agreement attempts to turn back the clock, it is important to note that this agreement does not change any laws. Despite the court’s order, Section 504, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the Supreme Court’s Olmstead decision remain in place. We continue to have the legal right to not be forced into institutions. It is very important that governors and attorneys general in every state understand that this order goes against decades of established law, and that the disability community will not go backwards. Although our legal right to live in the community remains in place, the federal government is taking away clear direction to the states that health and social services should support disabled people in community settings whenever appropriate. The removal of the community integration provisions of the HHS Section 504 rule applies to all states, not just the states that sued. Loss of this clear guidance is a serious setback for our work to ensure that people are not forced to live in institutions in order to get the services they need. Let’s be clear. Disability rights and our ability to live in our homes and our communities are in crisis. Although some states have expressed a commitment to ensuring that people with disabilities can live in the community, many states have not done so. We urge state legislatures to use this misguided and harmful ruling as a wake up call to enshrine the right of disabled people to live in their communities in state law. The rights of disabled people have been won at enormous costs by activists over the past 50 years. Disability rights are human rights. DCIC is a national coalition of organizations led by and for people with disabilities, focused on defending our right to live in the community. Stay tuned for updates from DCIC for action opportunities to defend our right to live in the community.
